questions.q: List four supporting characters from "Indigo" and state one specific action each takes in the narrative.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Rajkumar Shukla — follows Gandhi to Lucknow, Cawnpore, Ahmedabad, Calcutta, and finally brings him to Champaran; (2) Rajendra Prasad — hosts Gandhi at his Patna house, later arrives with lawyers to support him in court; (3) Professor Malkani — shelters Gandhi in his government quarters despite risk; (4) Charles Freer Andrews — offers to stay and help, but Gandhi refuses to teach self-reliance. A wrong answer (e.g., naming only Gandhi, or listing characters without actions) reveals the student treats supporting characters as names to memorise rather than agents who drive the narrative. This indicates a surface-level reading that misses how Fischer uses minor figures to build the Champaran movement's collective portrait.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Rajkumar Shukla is described as "resolute" and how his resoluteness functions in the narrative structure of "Indigo."
questions.a: Correct answer: Shukla is "resolute" because despite being illiterate and poor, he tracks Gandhi across multiple cities for weeks, waits at the appointed spot in Calcutta, and refuses to leave until Gandhi commits to a date. Narratively, he functions as the catalyst — without his persistence, Gandhi never reaches Champaran. His resoluteness mirrors the peasants' latent determination and foreshadows the mass courage that later surrounds the courthouse. A wrong answer (e.g., "he was stubborn" or "he wanted help") shows the student confuses personality trait with narrative function. The student misses that Shukla's tenacity is the structural hinge on which the entire Champaran episode turns — a classic "inciting incident" carried by a marginalised figure.

questions.q: Apply the "foil" concept to analyse how the Muzzafarpur lawyers' initial behaviour (charging high fees) contrasts with their later transformation (offering to go to jail with Gandhi). What does this contrast reveal about Gandhi's leadership?
questions.a: Correct answer: Initially, the lawyers act as a foil — they represent conventional, fee-based legalism that Gandhi explicitly rejects ("law courts are useless" for fear-stricken peasants). Their transformation into volunteers willing to court arrest becomes a measure of Gandhi's moral authority: he converts professionals invested in the colonial system into civil resisters. The contrast reveals that Gandhi's leadership operates not through hierarchy but through ethical example — he shames them into alignment ("shameful desertion"). A wrong answer (e.g., "lawyers changed their mind" without linking to Gandhi's method) shows the student can track plot but cannot analyse character as a thematic instrument. This is the difference between summarising and analysing.

questions.q: Compare Professor Malkani and Charles Freer Andrews as supporting characters who offer Gandhi shelter/help. How do their differing identities (Indian government teacher vs English pacifist) and Gandhi's responses to them advance the theme of self-reliance?
questions.a: Correct answer: Malkani, an Indian government employee, risks his job to "harbour a man like me" — his quiet defiance embodies indigenous courage. Andrews, an Englishman, offers solidarity, but Gandhi refuses: "You should not seek a prop in Mr. Andrews because he happens to be an Englishman." The contrast sharpens the theme: self-reliance means rejecting both colonial patronage (Andrews) and colonial fear (Malkani's risk). Gandhi accepts Malkani's help because it springs from Indian agency; he rejects Andrews' to prevent psychological dependence on white validation. A wrong answer (e.g., "both helped Gandhi") flattens the ideological distinction. The student misses that Fischer deliberately pairs these figures to dramatise the internal dimension of freedom — political independence requires psychological independence first.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The British officials in 'Indigo' (commissioner, magistrate, Lieutenant-Governor) are not villains but functionaries whose procedural rigidity exposes the moral bankruptcy of colonial rule." Support your evaluation with two textual instances.
questions.a: Correct answer: The claim is largely valid. The commissioner "bullies" Gandhi and orders him to leave Tirhut — not from personal malice but to maintain control. The magistrate follows procedure (summons, bail, recess) but is baffled by Gandhi's polite defiance ("officials felt powerless without Gandhi's cooperation"). The Lieutenant-Governor ultimately appoints a commission and drops the case — not from justice but because the system cannot handle non-violent non-cooperation. These men are cogs; their rigidity makes Gandhi's moral victory visible. A wrong answer (e.g., "they were evil British officers") reduces colonialism to individual villainy, missing Fischer's (and Gandhi's) deeper point: the system produces injustice even through "lawful" functionaries. This misreading weakens board answers on "Gandhi's method" and competitive-exam questions on colonial discourse.

questions.q: Write a 100-word diary entry from Kasturbai's perspective during the Champaran stay, reflecting on teaching sanitation to women who own only one sari. Use textual details to show her empathy and the theme of constructive work alongside political struggle.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (a) adopt Kasturbai's voice (observant, practical, compassionate); (b) include the specific detail — "the sari I am wearing is the only one I have"; (c) connect sanitation lessons to dignity, not just hygiene; (d) reflect Gandhian philosophy — constructive programme as foundation for freedom. Example opening: "April 1917, Champaran. Today a woman took me into her hut — no box, no cupboard, one sari. I taught her to wash it, dry it, wear it clean. She smiled. Bapu says freedom begins here, in clean corners and clean minds. The peasants fear the planters, but they fear dirt less. We will build schools, dig latrines, spin khadi. The British can jail Bapu, but they cannot jail this quiet revolution in our huts." A weak answer (generic "helped women," no textual anchor) shows the student cannot inhabit a supporting character's perspective or link micro-detail to macro-theme.
